subject: 인과는 규칙성인가 힘인가
title: Causation as regularity or as power
content: We say that striking a match causes it to light, and philosophy has asked what this relation consists in. One tradition holds that causation is nothing more than regular succession, so the claim asserts that events of the first kind are reliably followed by events of the second. This account is austere and it fits what observation delivers, since we see the striking and the flame but never any connection between them. Its difficulty is that regular succession occurs where nobody would speak of causation. Night follows day without being caused by it, and a falling barometer precedes a storm without producing one, so the account must add conditions to exclude such cases. Each addition has proved either too weak to exclude them or strong enough to smuggle in the notion it was avoiding. A rival tradition treats causation as the exercise of a power, so a cause makes its effect happen rather than merely preceding it. This matches how we think and it commits us to something that observation does not reveal. Recent work has tried a third route, analysing causation through what would have happened otherwise, and this handles many cases while struggling where several sufficient causes are present at once.

subject: 건강과 질병의 경계
title: Where health ends and disease begins
content: Calling a condition a disease has consequences, since it licenses treatment, entitles a person to care, and may excuse her from obligations. Philosophy of medicine therefore asks what makes a condition a disease, and the answers divide over whether the judgment is descriptive or evaluative. A naturalist account defines disease as departure from normal functioning for the organism's kind and stage, which makes the judgment a biological matter that inspection could settle. Its appeal is that it keeps medicine free of contested values. Its difficulty is that normality is statistical, so a common impairment counts as healthy while a rare beneficial variation counts as diseased, and neither verdict is acceptable. A normativist account defines disease as a condition we have reason to want treated, which handles those cases directly. The cost is that medical classification becomes openly evaluative, so disputes about whether a condition is a disease become disputes about what kind of life is good. Historical cases where classification tracked prejudice rather than biology are usually cited on both sides, since one reads them as showing the danger of values while the other reads them as showing that values were operating unacknowledged.

subject: 감상과 도덕적 결함의 관계
title: Moral flaws in works we admire
content: A novel may be well made and also endorse something repellent, and aesthetics asks whether the moral defect is an aesthetic defect too. The question is not whether we may criticize the work morally, which nobody denies, but whether the moral failing makes it worse as art. Autonomists hold that the two assessments are independent, so a work can be excellent aesthetically while being morally objectionable, and confusing the two leads to bad criticism. Their opponents argue that a moral defect can be an aesthetic one where it undermines what the work is trying to do. If a narrative invites us to find a cruelty amusing and we cannot, then the work has failed to secure the response it needs, and that failure is aesthetic however it arose. This account explains why some morally troubling works remain powerful while others collapse, since the difference lies in whether the response was actually blocked. A third position holds that moral flaws can even be aesthetic merits, because a work that makes us feel what we would rather not feel has achieved something. All three agree that the two dimensions interact, and they differ about which direction the influence runs.

subject: 후회의 합리성
title: When regret makes sense
content: Regret directs itself at what cannot be changed, and this has led some philosophers to call it irrational, since no action can follow from it and the suffering it causes is therefore pointless. The argument has force and it does not match how we assess people, because someone who feels nothing after causing serious harm strikes us as morally defective rather than admirably rational. Several accounts explain why. One holds that regret expresses a continuing commitment to the value that was violated, so a person who has wronged another shows by her regret that she still holds the standard she failed. Feeling nothing would indicate that the standard had gone. On this view regret is backward-looking in its object and forward-looking in what it reveals. A second account points to cases where the agent did nothing wrong. A driver who kills a child who ran into the road is not blameworthy, and yet we expect her to feel something more than an observer would, and a person who did not would seem to have missed her own involvement. Philosophers call this agent-regret, and its existence suggests that our moral responses track participation rather than fault alone.

subject: 고대 무덤의 방위와 천문
title: Ancient tombs and the directions they face
content: Many ancient tombs are lined up with a compass direction so exactly that chance cannot explain it, and archaeologists measure these bearings across whole cemeteries. Where a group of burials shares a bearing that differs from the lie of the land, that direction was chosen rather than forced by the ground. What the chosen direction refers to is the harder question. Some tombs point to sunrise at a solstice, and where the skyline is marked by a distinct hill the match can be checked against the sun's position for that period. Others point to no event in the sky but agree with a nearby monument, so they refer to the built landscape instead. Telling these apart means modelling the ancient skyline as it stood, since erosion and trees have changed it since. The reading must stay careful. A bearing shows that a direction mattered without showing why, and archaeologists have learned to distrust accounts that assume one meaning across regions. What the measurements do support is that these ancient groups were placing their dead on purpose, and that the thing they aimed at differed from place to place in ways the dug evidence can sometimes recover.

subject: 동정과 공정의 긴장
title: Compassion against fairness
content: Compassion moves us toward the person in front of us, and fairness requires treating like cases alike, so the two pull apart whenever a vivid case competes with an unseen one. A doctor who gives extra time to a distressed patient takes it from others waiting, and a donor who funds a named child leaves an anonymous many unfunded. Moral philosophy has examined whether compassion should be disciplined by fairness or whether fairness misdescribes what morality requires. Those who favour discipline point out that compassion tracks salience rather than need, so it systematically favours the near, the identifiable, and the sympathetic. An institution built on it would distribute badly, and the people it neglected would have a legitimate complaint that nobody had considered them. Those who resist reply that a morality reduced to impartial calculation loses what makes moral response moral. Compassion is not merely a heuristic for finding need; it is the recognition of another person as mattering, and a system that treats individuals as interchangeable units has lost that. Most workable positions assign compassion to individual relationships and fairness to institutions, while conceding that the boundary is neither sharp nor stable.

subject: 고대 전차의 구조와 전술
title: Ancient chariots and how they were used
content: Chariots recovered from ancient burials show construction of remarkable lightness, with bent-wood frames, spoked wheels, and platforms small enough for two. Reconstructions built to the excavated dimensions weigh far less than their appearance in later art suggests, and this changes what they could have done on a battlefield. A vehicle of that weight could move quickly over flat ground and would break apart in rough terrain. The tactical implications follow from the engineering. A light chariot carrying a driver and an archer functioned as a mobile platform for missiles rather than as a shock weapon, since driving it into massed infantry would have destroyed it. Ancient texts describing chariot warfare are consistent with this once the vehicles are understood, and the passages that seemed to describe charges turn out to describe passes at a distance. Their expense limited who could field them. A chariot required specialist woodworkers, trained horses, and a driver who had practised for years, so the vehicles appear in ancient records alongside the households that could sustain them. Historians therefore treat chariot burials as evidence about social hierarchy as much as about warfare, since the ability to maintain one marked a position that few could hold.

subject: 사고실험의 증거적 지위
title: What thought experiments establish
content: Philosophers reason from imagined cases, asking what we would say about a person whose brain is gradually replaced or a bystander who could divert a runaway trolley. Critics observe that nothing is observed in such cases and that the conclusions therefore rest on nothing more than what the philosopher finds plausible. Defenders answer that the same objection would condemn mathematical reasoning, which also proceeds without observation. The interesting question is what a thought experiment does. One account treats it as an argument in narrative form, so the imagined case makes vivid a premise that could be stated plainly, and the story is a presentational device rather than a source of evidence. This account is deflationary and it explains why some thought experiments can be paraphrased without loss. A second account holds that they do more, allowing us to detect consequences of our own commitments that abstract statement would conceal. On this view the case functions as a probe, revealing that we hold a principle we had not noticed or that two principles we accept conflict. Both accounts agree that a thought experiment is only as good as the intuitions it elicits, and that unstable intuitions make the method unreliable in exactly the cases where it is most used.

subject: 선험적 지식은 존재하는가
title: Whether anything can be known in advance of experience
content: Some claims seem knowable without investigation, among them that nothing is both red and green all over, and that a whole is larger than its parts. Philosophy calls such knowledge a priori and disputes both its extent and its possibility, since knowing something about the world without consulting the world requires explanation. One account grounds it in meaning. Such claims are true by what the words mean, so understanding them is sufficient for knowing them, and no investigation is needed because nothing about the world is being asserted. This handles definitional cases and it strains with mathematics, where the claims seem substantial rather than merely verbal. A second account appeals to a special faculty of rational insight, which many find obscure. Empiricists deny the category entirely, holding that even mathematical claims are revisable in the light of experience and that their apparent necessity reflects only how central they are to our thinking. Evidence from the history of science, where geometrical claims once thought necessary were revised, is usually cited here. What the debate has settled is that unrevisability cannot be the mark of the a priori, since almost nothing has proved unrevisable.

subject: 고대 유적의 화산재 층과 연대 확정
title: Volcanic ash and dating ancient sites
content: A volcanic eruption spreads a layer of ash across a wide area within days, and that layer settles into the ground everywhere at once. For archaeologists this creates a marker of extraordinary value, since anything below it predates the eruption and anything above it follows, and the same layer can be identified at sites hundreds of kilometres apart. Chemical fingerprinting makes the identification secure. Ash from different eruptions differs in the composition of its glass shards, so a sample taken from a site can be matched to a specific event rather than merely to volcanic activity in general. Where the eruption itself has been dated by other means, every site containing its ash inherits that date. This has resolved chronologies that decades of relative dating had left uncertain. The method has changed how ancient sequences are compared. Before it, sites in different regions were correlated by matching pottery styles, which assumed that styles spread quickly and uniformly. Ash layers test that assumption directly, and in several cases they have shown styles persisting far longer in one region than in another. Archaeologists therefore treat these layers as one of the few genuinely independent checks available on ancient chronology.

subject: 존재하지 않는 것이 더 나은 경우
title: Whether it can be better never to exist
content: Some philosophers argue that coming into existence is always a harm, since a life contains suffering that could have been avoided by not existing, while the goods it contains are not missed by anyone who never exists. The argument rests on an asymmetry, holding that the absence of pain is good whether or not anyone enjoys that absence, while the absence of pleasure is not bad unless someone is deprived. Stated that way the asymmetry seems plausible, and its consequences are extreme. Critics attack the asymmetry directly. If absent pain is good for nobody, they argue, then the goodness has no bearer and the comparison collapses, whereas if we allow goods and harms to attach to non-existent people then absent pleasure should count as bad by the same reasoning. The asymmetry appears to be assumed rather than defended. Defenders reply that our ordinary judgments support it, since we think it wrong to create a life of certain misery while we do not think it obligatory to create a life of certain happiness. This observation is genuine and it may be explained without the strong conclusion, since duties not to harm are widely held to be weightier than duties to benefit, and that distinction does the same work without implying that existence is always a wrong.

subject: 고대 신전 건축의 채석과 운반
title: Quarrying and hauling for ancient temples
content: The stone of an ancient temple came from a quarry that can often be identified, since its geology matches a specific outcrop and the quarry floor keeps the hollows left by what was taken. Blocks abandoned in place, some of them cracked and some simply never moved, show the order of work and the tools that did it. A quarry therefore records the building as directly as the temple does. Moving the stone was the harder problem. These blocks travelled by sledge on prepared trackways, by water where a river or coast allowed it, and up ramps whose earthen remains survive beside several ancient sites. Experiments have established the crews needed, and their figures make the hauling rather than the carving the largest cost of such a project. Route choice therefore decided where a temple could stand at all. What this evidence reveals about organization is considerable. Feeding and housing a haulage crew through a season demanded stores, and the settlements built for that purpose have been dug near several ancient quarries. Historians accordingly read a temple as the visible end of a system whose other parts were quarrymen, hauliers, victuallers, and the officials who held them together across years.

subject: 신뢰와 취약성의 구조
title: Trust and the vulnerability it requires
content: Trusting someone involves relying on her while accepting that she could let you down, and this exposure is what distinguishes trust from mere prediction. A person who has arranged matters so that betrayal is impossible is not trusting; she is managing risk. Philosophy has therefore treated vulnerability as constitutive rather than incidental. What follows is that trust cannot be replaced by verification without changing into something else. Systems designed to make betrayal impossible eliminate the need for trust and eliminate its benefits along with it, since a relationship in which each party monitors the other continuously is not one in which either is trusted. Institutions that increase monitoring often find that the behaviour they wanted decreases, which this analysis predicts. Trust also carries a moral dimension that reliance lacks. Being trusted is being counted on in a way that creates a reason to perform, so betrayal wrongs the truster rather than merely disappointing her, and the resentment that follows differs from the annoyance of a failed prediction. Philosophers disagree about what generates this reason, with some grounding it in the truster's reliance and others in a relationship the two parties share. The disagreement matters where trust is extended to strangers or to institutions.

subject: 고대 도시 성문의 구조와 통제
title: Ancient city gates and what passed through them
content: An ancient city gate was more than an opening, and excavation shows structures of considerable depth, with chambers flanking a passage that turned at least once so that attackers could not charge straight through. Those chambers held guards, and the benches built into them appear in enough examples to indicate a standard arrangement rather than a local preference. Their other function was administrative. Goods entering a city were assessed at the gate, so the chambers held officials as well as guards, and the ancient documents recovered near several gates concern exactly this business. Weights and sealings found in the deposits confirm what the texts describe, and the wear on the paving records the traffic that passed. The gate was where a city touched the countryside. It also served as a public space. Ancient sources describe legal proceedings held at the gate, and the benches that archaeologists interpret as guard seating would have served that purpose equally. Historians reading these structures therefore treat them as the point where defence, taxation, and justice met, and the elaboration of a gate as evidence about how much a community needed to control what came in.

subject: 고대의 도로 포장 기술과 유지
title: Ancient road surfaces and keeping them usable
content: Sections cut through ancient roads reveal building in layers, with large stones set as a base, smaller material above them, and a running surface of gravel or fitted slabs on top. Their depth varies with the ground beneath, so the builders were reading conditions rather than following one recipe, and the ditches cut alongside show that water was understood as their main enemy. What excavation also reveals is repair. These surfaces were relaid again and again, and the layers can be counted and sometimes dated, so a road records the centuries through which someone kept it up. Where those layers stop, the upkeep stopped, and the soil above shows the road being ploughed over or built upon. That break is often sharper than the written sources suggest. Its cost fell on whoever gained. Ancient records describe duties laid on nearby communities to keep their stretch usable, and the quality seen in excavation varies between neighbouring sections in ways that suggest uneven compliance. Historians therefore read an ancient road as a chain of local duties held together by a power that could enforce them, and its decay as evidence that the enforcement had lapsed rather than that the route was forgotten.

subject: 고대 도자기의 형식 편년
title: Dating the ancient past by pottery form
content: Pottery survives when almost nothing else does, and its shapes change steadily, so archaeologists have long used vessel form to date the layers in which it appears. The method assumes that styles develop gradually and that a given form belongs to a limited period, and it was built by observing which types occur together in sealed deposits across many ancient sites. Refinement came from stratigraphy. Where one layer lies above another, its pottery is later, and assembling many such observations produces a sequence that holds regardless of what the absolute dates turn out to be. Radiocarbon dating and volcanic ash layers have since supplied those absolute anchors, and the two methods largely agree, which is a substantial check on both. The limits are worth stating plainly. A style may persist longer in one region than another, so a form dated at one ancient site can mislead at a distant one, and residual sherds from earlier occupation contaminate later layers. Archaeologists therefore date a deposit by the latest material it contains rather than by the commonest, and they treat regional sequences as separate until independent evidence links them.

subject: 고대 요새의 입지 선정
title: Where ancient fortresses were placed
content: Ancient fortresses sit on hills, at river crossings, and at the mouths of valleys, and mapping their positions reveals a logic that the individual sites do not disclose. A fortress on a hill that overlooks nothing important is rare, whereas a modest structure commanding a single practicable route is common, which indicates that control of movement rather than elevation was the criterion. Analysis of visibility has made this precise. Modelling what could be seen from each site shows chains of fortresses in which each is visible from the next, so a signal could pass along a whole frontier within hours. Where such a chain exists, the individual structures were parts of a system, and dating them shows whether the system was built at once or assembled over generations. The excavated evidence sometimes contradicts the strategic reading. A well-placed fortress may show brief occupation and no destruction, which suggests it was abandoned for reasons unrelated to any attack, and the ancient sources occasionally record exactly that. Historians therefore combine the spatial analysis with the excavation of each site, since position explains what a fortress was for while the deposits explain what actually happened there.

subject: 고대 항구의 방파제와 준설
title: Ancient harbour works and the silt that filled them
content: Ancient harbours were built where nature provided shelter, and where it did not, moles of stone or concrete were run out into open water to create it. Underwater survey has mapped these structures at many sites, and the techniques used differ enough between regions to show independent solutions to the same problem. Some were built of quarried blocks lowered into place and some of hydraulic concrete poured into forms. Every harbour then faced the same enemy. Sheltered water drops the sediment it carries, so the basin that a mole created began filling from the day it was finished, and dredging was required continuously. Cores taken through harbour deposits record this history directly, since the layers alternate between accumulation and the sharp truncations that dredging leaves. Where the truncations stop, the maintenance stopped. That moment is often the most informative thing a harbour excavation yields. A silted basin puts a port out of use whatever its political importance, and several ancient cities that declined without any recorded disaster show exactly this sequence. Historians therefore examine harbour cores before attributing a port's decline to war or to trade, since the sediment may already contain the answer.

subject: 고대 청동 거울의 제작과 분포
title: Ancient bronze mirrors and where they travelled
content: Bronze mirrors from ancient burials were cast in moulds, polished on one face, and decorated on the other, and the decoration is distinctive enough that regional workshops can be told apart. Because the alloy composition also varies by workshop, chemical analysis confirms attributions that style alone would leave uncertain, and the two lines of evidence together map where each type was made. Their distribution runs far beyond the regions that produced them. Mirrors turn up in graves hundreds of kilometres from their workshop, often as the single imported object among otherwise local goods, which indicates that they moved as valued items rather than as ordinary trade. Where local imitations appear, they can be identified by alloy and by errors in the decoration, and their presence marks the point at which an imported form became a model. What the burials add is context. A mirror placed with a body says something about how the object was regarded, and its position in the grave differs between regions in ways that suggest different meanings attached to the same artefact. Archaeologists therefore treat these mirrors as evidence about ancient contact and about what travelled with an object besides the object itself.

subject: 선사 무덤군의 배치와 친족
title: Prehistoric cemeteries and the kin who used them
content: Prehistoric cemeteries are rarely laid out at random, and their order is the first thing an excavator notices. Graves gather in clusters, and those clusters are parted by empty ground that later burials respect, which shows that the people using a cemetery knew where earlier graves lay and therefore chose to place their dead beside particular ones. Archaeologists have long read such clusters as family groups, although until recently that reading rested on the layout alone. Ancient genomes have now tested it directly. Where bone survives well enough, the ties within a cemetery can be worked out, and the results sometimes confirm the spatial reading while sometimes upsetting it. Clusters that looked like families have turned out to hold unrelated people, whereas close kin have been found buried far apart, so nearness encoded something other than descent at those sites. What the combined evidence supports is that burial placement followed groupings whose basis varied. In some prehistoric communities those groupings were kin, in others they were households holding unrelated members, and in others the ordering principle is still unclear. Archaeologists therefore no longer read a cluster as a family without testing, because the cases where the test fails have proved the most telling.

subject: 중세 촌락의 소실과 재정착
title: Medieval villages that vanished
content: Thousands of medieval villages were left empty, and their sites survive as earthworks in fields that were never built on again. Aerial survey reveals house platforms, sunken lanes worn by traffic, and the edges of plots, so the plan of a whole settlement can be recovered without digging. The clearness of these remains makes them among the best evidence we have for how medieval villagers actually lived. Explaining why they emptied has proved harder than mapping them. Plague is the obvious cause and it fits some cases badly, since excavation shows several villages living through the worst decades and failing generations later. Others were cleared on purpose when landowners turned ploughland to pasture, and the written record names those cases. A third group simply shifted a short way, so the village went on while its site moved. Telling these apart means dating the last occupation closely, and pottery from the final phases supplies that. Where the dates gather in the decades after a plague, mortality is likely; where they spread across a century, a slower process was at work. Historians therefore treat medieval desertion as several distinct things that the landscape records in the same way.

subject: 고대 유적에서 나온 직물의 흔적
title: Traces of ancient cloth
content: Textiles decay almost everywhere, so ancient cloth survives only in waterlogged, frozen, or extremely dry conditions, and the resulting sample is heavily skewed toward a few regions. Archaeologists therefore work mostly from traces rather than from fabric, and the traces are more informative than their slightness suggests. Corrosion on a bronze object can preserve the imprint of the cloth it lay against, recording weave, thread count, and sometimes the direction of spin. Tools supply another line. Spindle whorls of different weights suit different fibres, and loom weights indicate the width of cloth being woven, so a settlement's textile production can be estimated from equipment even where no fabric survives. Seeds of fibre plants and the bones of wool-bearing animals add further evidence, and the three together allow a reconstruction that no single source would support. What this evidence establishes is scale. The number of spindle whorls at many ancient sites implies that spinning occupied a substantial part of available labour, probably more than any other craft, and that most of it was done in households rather than workshops. Historians accordingly treat cloth production as a major and largely invisible sector of the ancient economy that the surviving artefacts barely represent.

subject: 고대의 활과 화살촉 형식 변천
title: Ancient bows and the changing shapes of arrowheads
content: Arrowheads survive in enormous numbers because stone and metal endure, and their shapes change through time in ways that archaeologists have catalogued in detail. The sequence supplies dating for sites that yield little else, and it also records something about how the weapon was used, since a broad head suits hunting while a narrow one is designed to defeat armour. Bows themselves rarely survive. Where waterlogging has preserved them, the wood, the profile, and occasionally the string material can be studied, and reconstructions built to those dimensions have been tested for draw weight and range. The results establish that ancient bows were considerably more powerful than the surviving arrowheads alone would suggest. Composite construction, using horn and sinew laminated to a wooden core, appears in several regions and required materials and skill that a simple bow did not. What the combined evidence shows is a technology under continuous pressure. Changes in arrowhead form follow changes in armour, and the appearance of composite bows correlates with contexts where range mattered more than convenience. Archaeologists therefore read these small objects as a record of an arms race whose other half has almost entirely decayed.

subject: 초기 금속기의 매납과 의례
title: Buried metalwork and what it was for
content: Hoards of early metalwork are found buried in ground that shows no settlement, often in bogs, rivers, or beneath boulders, and explaining them has divided archaeologists for a long time. One reading treats them as property hidden in danger and never recovered, which would make each hoard a record of some local emergency. That reading fits some deposits and not others. Many hoards contain objects deliberately broken or bent before burial, which is difficult to reconcile with an intention to retrieve them, and the places chosen are frequently wet ground from which recovery would be hard. The distribution also clusters at boundaries and at confluences rather than near dwellings. These features have led most researchers to read such deposits as offerings rather than as savings. What complicates the picture is that the two explanations need not compete across a whole region. Some hoards show the signs of ritual treatment and others do not, and the same landscape can contain both, so the interpretation must be made deposit by deposit. Archaeologists therefore examine the condition of the objects and the character of the findspot before deciding, and they report the cases that remain ambiguous as ambiguous.
